newsitem.title: GERMANY: No pressure on Kohl for decision-coalition partner.
newsitem.headline: No pressure on Kohl for decision-coalition partner.

text.p: Germany's liberal Free Democrats said on Tuesday they were not pressing Chancellor Helmut Kohl for a quick decision on whether to stand in the 1998 election, despite reports he was coming under pressure from his allies.

Disagreement within the coalition over major tax and pension reforms intended to win it next year's election, as well as a sense of helplessness over runaway unemployment, have added to speculation that Kohl, 66, may not see out his term.
A report in the daily Die Welt said Kohl's allies in the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) were pressing him to make a decision, preferably to stay on, within the next eight weeks.

But Hermann Otto Solms, the parliamentary leader of the FDP, told Berlin's Info Radio: "Kohl doesn't need to make a decision about his candidacy yet. It can remain open until the autumn... We need to sort out policies, that's much more important."

And FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhardt told Die Welt, according to an advance release from Wednesday's edition, that he believed "...Helmut Kohl will be the Christian Democrats' next chancellery candidate, whenever he announces his decision."
But chairman of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) Oskar Lafontaine said Kohl was doing himself no favours by leaving the question open.

"A head of government who leaves it open for so long whether he will stand again, will increasingly become a lame duck," Lafontaine told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung in an interview released ahead of publication on Wednesday.
The pressure is mounting on Europe's longest serving head of government to show he still has what it takes to revive flagging public confidence in his government and his own personal authority.
Members of his party have gone public with astonishingly frank disagreements over taxes and pensions in the last month, suggesting Kohl has lost some of his famed internal control.

Many analysts say weakness on Kohl's part could have repercussions for European monetary union (EMU) in 1999, a project which may require the full authority of the chancellor of 14 years to convince a sceptical German public.
On Sunday Kohl told French television he had not yet made up his mind but would ponder whether to stay on after June's European Union reform summit in Amsterdam.
A CSU spokesman declined to comment on the report in Die Welt, which said party leaders were irritated that Kohl had left matters so open, rather than avoiding the question.
The paper said the FDP was also unhappy with the comment and that the CSU was concerned about the unsettling effect of worries about Kohl's health.

The weekly Der Spiegel noted in Monday's edition that Kohl has received treatment four times in eight years for prostate problems including the removal of a benign tumour, although Kohl's office emphatically denies he has cancer.
That issue remains taboo for coalition politicians.

But some, such as Lower Saxony CDU leader Christian Wulff, are pushing publicly for fast action on other issues including the tax and pensions reforms which have pitted parts of the CDU against each other.
Wulff said that if parliament could not agree on the key issues by the end of the spring then its summer recess should be cancelled.
Spring is traditionally a time when Kohl comes back from his Easter holiday in Austria refreshed and ready with new initiatives -- something his political allies will be keenly awaiting this year.
Gerhardt, too, said the next few months would be crucial.

"Delayed reforms, resistance, denial of global developments, putting off tough decisions. The discussion in the CDU reflects social conflicts as a whole. This is something we'll have to get through this spring. Then prospects will become clearer."
